lesson.title: Rising Scores: The Flynn Effect and What It Reveals About Nature and Nurture
lesson.summary: Raw IQ scores rose substantially across generations through much of the twentieth century, a well documented pattern named for James Flynn that offers strong evidence for environmental influence on measured intelligence.
lesson.body:
One of the most well documented and, at first glance, surprising findings in the history of intelligence testing is that raw scores on IQ tests rose substantially across successive generations throughout the twentieth century, in country after country where records have been carefully tracked. This pattern is named after the researcher James Flynn, who compiled and analyzed data showing that if people today took an IQ test that was normed decades ago, they would score notably higher on average than the original standardization sample did, and the reverse holds too: people from decades ago, if they could take a modern test, would tend to score below average by today's norms.

Because IQ tests are deliberately normed so that the standardization sample averages a score of 100, as explained in the earlier chapter on IQ and mental age, this generational rise means that test publishers have had to periodically renorm their tests, raising the bar for what raw performance counts as an average score of 100. Historically, the size of this rise has often been estimated at roughly three IQ points per decade in many industrialized countries during much of the twentieth century, though the exact rate has varied by country, by time period, and by which specific subtests are examined.

Notably, the gains have not been uniform across all types of test content. They tend to be larger on tests of fluid reasoning, such as the Raven's Progressive Matrices, which asks test takers to identify abstract patterns rather than draw on specific learned knowledge, and smaller on tests that depend more heavily on accumulated vocabulary or factual knowledge. This pattern has shaped debate over what is actually driving the effect, with proposed explanations including improved childhood nutrition and reduced disease burden, expanded access to formal schooling, smaller family sizes, and a broader cultural shift toward more abstract, hypothetical, and scientific styles of thinking that modern life and education increasingly demand.

The Flynn effect connects directly to the nature versus nurture debate. A genuine shift of this size within just a few generations happens far too quickly to be explained by changes in the underlying gene pool, since meaningful genetic change in a population typically requires many more generations to unfold. This makes the Flynn effect one of the clearest pieces of evidence that measured intelligence, whatever its biological basis, remains substantially responsive to environmental conditions, which complicates any simple story that treats IQ scores as a fixed, purely inherited trait.

It is also worth noting, with appropriate caution, that some more recent research has suggested the rise may be slowing or even reversing in a handful of countries, particularly in parts of Scandinavia, since roughly the final decades of the twentieth century, though researchers are still working out how widespread, reliable, and well explained this apparent reversal actually is.
